name: Queen's Indian Defense
summary: The Queen's Indian Defence (1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6) fianchettoes to b7 to fight for the light squares and e4; solid and flexible.
intro: The Queen's Indian Defence is reached after 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6, a solid and flexible hypermodern system in which Black fianchettoes the queen's bishop to b7. From there the bishop fights for control of the central light squares, above all e4, and dovetails naturally with the Nimzo-Indian when White develops the knight to f3 instead of c3.
line: d4 Nf6 c4 e6 Nf3 b6

sections.heading: Strategic ideas
paragraphs: The Queen's Indian is built around the fianchetto of the queen's bishop to b7, from where it contests the long light-squared diagonal and, in particular, the e4-square. After 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nf3 b6, Black adopts a restrained, hypermodern approach: instead of staking out the centre with pawns, he keeps a compact, resilient structure and relies on precise piece placement to blunt White's central ambitions. The result is one of the soundest and most reliable defences to 1.d4.

The battle usually revolves around the e4-square and the light squares generally. Black often supports his grip with ...Bb7, ...Be7 or ...Bb4+, ...d5 or ...c5, and sometimes the manoeuvre ...Ne4 to trade pieces and ease his position. White, for his part, tries to expand in the centre with e4 or to seize space and outpost his pieces. Because the structures remain flexible, the Queen's Indian is prized as a low-risk, strategically deep choice.

sections.heading: Main variations
paragraphs: The main line is 4.g3, when White meets the fianchetto with his own, playing Bg2 to fight for the light squares from the other side. Black's most testing reply is 4...Ba6, immediately pressuring the c4-pawn and provoking a concession, though the classical 4...Bb7 followed by ...Be7 and ...O-O remains fully respectable. These positions are rich in subtle manoeuvring around the central squares.

White's other main try is 4.a3, the Petrosian Variation, which prevents ...Bb4 and prepares Nc3 and e4 with a free hand in the centre; Black usually responds with ...d5 or ...Bb7 and ...c5. After 4.Nc3, Black can steer toward Nimzo-Indian structures with 4...Bb4, so the Queen's Indian and Nimzo-Indian form two halves of a single, interlocking repertoire against 1.d4 and 2.c4.

sections.heading: History and background
paragraphs: The Queen's Indian grew out of the hypermodern revolution of the 1920s, and Aron Nimzowitsch was among its most influential early advocates, applying his ideas about central control and blockade to the queenside fianchetto. The name reflects that it is an Indian-style defence developing on the queen's wing.

It became a cornerstone of top-level opening play, especially valued as Black's answer when White sidesteps the Nimzo-Indian with 3.Nf3. Generations of elite players, including World Champions such as Anatoly Karpov and Garry Kasparov, have relied on it for its blend of solidity and long-term strategic richness.

keyIdeas: Black fianchettoes the queen's bishop to b7 to fight for the light squares.
Control of the e4-square is the central strategic theme.
A solid, flexible, low-risk system that avoids early pawn commitments.
...Ba6 hits the c4-pawn and is the critical try against 4.g3.
...Ne4 is a typical manoeuvre to trade pieces and relieve pressure.
The natural partner to the Nimzo-Indian when White plays 3.Nf3.

white: Fianchetto with g3 and Bg2 to contest the long light diagonal.
Prepare and play e4 to build a central pawn advantage.
Choose 4.a3 (Petrosian) to rule out ...Bb4 before playing Nc3 and e4.
Gain space and seek outposts while Black stays compact.
Exchange or restrict the b7-bishop to loosen Black's light-square grip.
black: Develop ...Bb7 to control e4 and the long diagonal.
Pressure c4 with ...Ba6 against the g3 systems.
Free the position with a timely ...d5 or ...c5 break.
Use ...Ne4 to trade pieces and ease any cramp.
Steer into Nimzo-Indian setups with ...Bb4 when White allows it.
